children: 0941 GMT - The dollar might struggle to rise unless the Federal Reserve cements expectations for an extended interest-rate rise cycle in a decision later, MUFG Bank's Lee Hardman says in a note. The market is nearly fully pricing a 25 basis-point rate rise Wednesday and almost 95 basis points of tightening by September 2027, LSEG data show. This pricing creates a high bar for the Fed to sound more "hawkish" in favor of raising rates than expected, Hardman says. The Fed's communication is unlikely to provide a clear signal over how much further tightening is likely to be needed, he says. The decision is at 1800 GMT. The DXY dollar index trades flat at 99.639. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0937 GMT - Investors' attention is on the U.S. Federal Reserve interest-rate decision due at 1800 GMT, where a rate increase is widely expected. However, traders will also pay attention to the Fed's communication and policymakers' commitment to tackling inflation over the coming months, Tickmill Group's Patrick Munnelly says in a note. "The broader reaction will be clearest in the dollar, gold and equities, where investors will quickly signal whether they see the Fed as regaining control or simply chasing a market that has already moved ahead of it," he says. Ten-year U.S. Treasurys rare last steady at 4.996%, having hit a 19-year high of 5.041% this week, LSEG data show. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0927 GMT - The euro could fall slightly against the dollar if the Federal Reserve raises interest rates and signals further possible tightening in a decision later, ING's Francesco Pesole says in a note. Looking further ahead, the Fed and European Central Bank are unlikely to deliver another rate rise, implying room for money markets to significantly reduce pricing of additional U.S. and eurozone rate increases, he says. This would limit the scope for the euro to fall. "A coordinated move lower in front-end rates can put a floor under euro-dollar, as would likely happen alongside a decline in energy prices." The euro trades flat at $1.1539 and ING expects it to reach $1.15 after the Fed decision at 1800 GMT. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0921 GMT - Weak credit transmission, prolonged property correction and subdued private demand are likely to prevent a meaningful recovery and constrain growth into 2027 for China, Julius Baer economist Sophie Altermatt writes in a note. China's economy remained highly uneven in August as stronger industrial production and robust exports contrasted with further weakness in consumption, investment and property activity, she adds. Weakening credit dynamics confirm a weak appetite for loans among households and businesses, she says. There will likely be faster fiscal execution to help stabilize growth toward year end, but not to generate a broad-based recovery, Julius Baer says. The bank maintains its 2026 GDP growth forecast at 4.5%, the low end of the official target range.(jiahui.huang@wsj.com; @ivy_jiahuihuang)

0916 GMT - The cost of insuring euro-denominated credit against default falls slightly as global markets sentiment stabilizes. Global stocks and government bonds trim the losses posted on Monday and Tuesday as focus is on the U.S. Federal Reserve interest-rate decision due at 1800 GMT. Investors widely expect the Fed to raise interest rates by a quarter point. Attention will also be on the Fed communication and any signals on potential interest-rate rises at future meetings. The iTraxx Europe Crossover index of euro high-yield credit default swaps falls 2 basis points to 263bps, S&P Global Market Intelligence data show. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0913 GMT - China's tepid GDP growth in August raises the probability of additional fiscal stimulus in 4Q, BNP Paribas economists say in a note. Based on the bank's estimates, real GDP growth last month was 4.3% on year. Policymakers may introduce new fiscal stimulus in October if 3Q growth slows to around 4.0% and if the economy fails to recover despite having support from fiscal measures. Economists say fresh stimulus measures may include more policy-based financial instruments, as fiscal policy is the most effective lever to counter short-term weak growth. (amanda.lee@wsj.com)

0911 GMT - Sterling could fall further against the euro as the latest U.K. inflation data might tilt the Bank of England towards dampening elevated interest-rate rise expectations in a decision Thursday, ING's Francesco Pesole says in a note. Data Wednesday showed inflation accelerated to 3.1% in August, as expected, but core and services inflation were unchanged. That supports the case for the BOE to sound cautious about raising rates, he says. "We still target a return above 0.8600 in euro/sterling in the coming days." The euro rises 0.1% to 0.8570 pounds. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0846 GMT - U.K. interest-rate rise expectations look excessive, leaving sterling at risk of falling, MUFG Bank's Lee Hardman says in a note. "The lack of second round inflation effects so far and continued weakness in the U.K. labor market is helping to ease some of the building pressure on the Bank of England to tighten policy." Although the BOE might struggle to look past headline inflation potentially reaching 4% in the new year unless energy prices ease, rate-rise expectations appear overdone, he says. Data Wednesday showed inflation rose to 3.1% in August, as forecast, but core inflation held at 2.6%. The euro rises 0.1% to 0.8567 pounds. Sterling is steady against the dollar at $1.3467. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0818 GMT - Investors slightly cut back their expectations of the Bank of England increasing interest rates over the coming months after the latest U.K. inflation data showed few signs of second-round inflation effects. Annual core inflation stayed unchanged at 2.6% in August, suggesting domestic inflation pressures remain steady. "The absence of clear second-round [inflation] effects gives policymakers room to avoid overreacting," Tickmill Group's Patrick Munnelly says in a note. Markets see an 19% chance of a BOE rate increase at Thursday's policy decision, down from 33% probability priced in on Tuesday, LSEG data show. Nonetheless, investors still fully price in four BOE rate increases over the coming year. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0811 GMT - The Clarity Act may return to the Senate but this is unlikely before the midterms, making the passage even more difficult depending on the election outcome, says Carsten Menke at Julius Baer. Opposition to the Act was unexpectedly broad, with Democrats and several Republicans voting against the bill. "A consistent regulatory framework would of course be welcome, but we would also argue that regulation does not drive adoption," Menke says in an email. Prediction markets are a case in point: While blockchain-based Polymarket was the early mover, it has been outgrown by non-blockchain-based Kalshi. Something similar could happen on trading platforms, Menke says. For now, crypto markets in the U.S. could operate based on a patchwork of existing rules, regulations, court decisions, and the already-enacted Genius Act for stablecoins. (monica.gupta@wsj.com)

0803 GMT - Hong Kong's first five-year plan marks a turning point in the city's economic landscape, says Marcos Chan, head of research at CBRE Hong Kong in a note. The plan includes nearly double the spending on technology and innovation. Chan says the city is diversifying its economy and paving the way for sustainable growth. Hong Kong needs a balanced model to support traditional industries and emerging tech sectors, he notes. This plan is also asking "business stakeholders to rethink their approach to future growth and re-formulate their business strategies," he says. (amanda.lee@wsj.com)

0737 GMT - Ether stays under pressure after reaching a two-week low Tuesday when the Senate failed to pass the Clarity Act, aimed at establishing a regulatory framework for digital assets, in a procedural vote. The market is also largely pricing in an interest-rate rise by the Federal Reserve in a decision at 1800 GMT. While ether exchange-traded funds are attracting inflows, large holders of ether--known as "whales"--have recently sold the cryptocurrency, Zaye Capital Markets analyst Naeem Aslam says in a note. If whale selling accelerates and ETF inflows weaken, ether could fall further, he says. Ether drops 0.4% to $2,398 after reaching as low as $2,359 Tuesday, LSEG data show. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)
